2.3 Feature Dynamics Distillation Feature Dynamics Distillation (FDD) (Gong et al., 2025) extends KD by viewing Transformer depth as discrete time steps of a continuous-depth dynamical system, following ODE-inspired interpretations of deep networks (Chen et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2019).
Inspired by the trajectory-based distillation framework of Gong et al. (2025), our approach departs from it by explicitly aligning the evolution of relational geometry across network depth.

While effective for capturing continuity in prediction dynamics, FDD aligns prediction dynamics using the same LM-head-based objective at the selected layers, without explicitly encoding depthdependent linguistic structure or salience-aware token weighting (Gong et al., 2025).
However, most existing approaches adopt a static and uniform alignment strategy across layers, typically operating at the token level.

By treating tokens largely in isolation and applying the same objective uniformly, these methods fail to account for differences in token importance and semantic roles across layers, which can harm generalization.

evidence.quote: To address this, we propose Autonomy-of-Expert (AoE), a novel MoE paradigm in which experts autonomously select themselves to process inputs.
In AoE, routers are removed; instead, experts pre-compute internal activations for inputs and are ranked based on their activation norms.
To address this, the concept of “expert autonomy” was proposed (Lv et al., 2025), wherein all experts process each token and those with the largest activation norm are selected.

In this paper, we introduce Union-of-Experts (UoE), an MoE framework designed to reconcile the benefits of expert autonomy with affordable computational overhead.
We provide both empirical and theoretical evidence that UoE is more efficient than AoE, the state-of-the-art expert autonomy practice.

evidence.quote: In this work we introduce a conversational forecasting model that learns an unsupervised representation of conversational dynamics and exploits it to predict future derailment as the conversation develops.

However, all existing models conflate belief estimation with decision-making by triggering alerts via a fixed threshold on the estimated probability of derailment, regardless of whether this probability is calculated via hierarchical recurrent neural networks (Chang and Danescu-NiculescuMizil, 2019), graph convolutional networks (Altarawneh et al., 2023), transformer architectures (Kementchedjhieva and Søgaard, 2021), hierarchical transformer architectures (Yuan and Singh, 2023), or LLM prompting (Olpadkar et al., 2025).
Incorporating this mechanism into a state-of-the-art forecasting model substantially reduces false positives without sacrificing forecasting accuracy.
Existing approaches make this decision solely based on the estimated likelihood of derailment given the preceding utterances, implicitly assuming that the conversation’s future trajectory is fixed.
